{{short description|Three-dimensional analog of the Pythagorean theorem}}

[[File:De_gua_theorem_1.svg|thumb|upright=1.4|Tetrahedron with a right-angle corner in O]]
In [[mathematics]], '''De Gua's theorem''' is a three-dimensional analog of the [[Pythagorean theorem]] named after [[Jean Paul de Gua de Malves]]. It states that if a [[tetrahedron]] has a right-angle corner (like the corner of a [[cube (geometry)|cube]]), then the square of the area of the face opposite the right-angle corner is the sum of the squares of the areas of the other three faces:
<math display="block"> A_{ABC}^2 = A_{\color {blue} ABO}^2+A_{\color {green} ACO}^2+A_{\color {red} BCO}^2 </math>De Gua's theorem can be applied for proving a special case of [[Heron's formula]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lévy-Leblond |first1=Jean-Marc |year=2020 |title=The Theorem of Cosines for Pyramids |journal=The Mathematical Intelligencer |publisher=SpringerLink|doi=10.1007/s00283-020-09996-8 |s2cid=224956341 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Generalizations==
The [[Pythagorean theorem]] and de Gua's theorem are special cases ({{math|1=''n'' = 2, 3}}) of a [[Simplex#Simplices with an "orthogonal corner"|general theorem]] about [[simplex|''n''-simplices]] with a [[right angle|right-angle]] corner, proved by P. S. Donchian and [[H. S. M. Coxeter]] in 1935.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Donchian |first1=P. S. |last2=Coxeter |first2=H. S. M. |date=July 1935 |title=1142. An n-dimensional extension of Pythagoras' Theorem |journal=The Mathematical Gazette |volume=19 |issue=234 |pages=206 |doi=10.2307/3605876|jstor=3605876 |s2cid=125391795 }}</ref> This, in turn, is a special case of [[Pythagorean theorem#Sets of m-dimensional objects in n-dimensional space|a yet more general theorem]] by Donald R. Conant and William A. Beyer (1974),<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.2307/2319528 |title=Generalized Pythagorean Theorem |author1=Donald R Conant  |author2=William A Beyer  |name-list-style=amp |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=81 |date=Mar 1974 |pages=262–265 |jstor=2319528 |issue=3 |publisher=Mathematical Association of America }}</ref> which can be stated as follows.

Let ''U'' be a [[Borel set|measurable]] subset of a ''k''-dimensional [[Affine space#Affine subspaces|affine subspace]] of <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> (so <math>k \le n</math>).  For any subset <math>I \subseteq \{ 1, \ldots, n \}</math> with exactly ''k'' elements, let <math>U_I</math> be the [[Projection (linear algebra)#Orthogonal projections|orthogonal projection]] of ''U'' onto the [[linear span]] of <math>e_{i_1}, \ldots, e_{i_k}</math>, where <math>I = \{i_1, \ldots, i_k\}</math> and <math>e_1, \ldots, e_n</math> is the [[standard basis]] for <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>.  Then
<math display="block">\operatorname{vol}_k^2(U) = \sum_I \operatorname{vol}_k^2(U_I),</math>
where <math>\operatorname{vol}_k(U)</math> is the [[Hausdorff measure|''k''-dimensional volume]] of ''U'' and the sum is over all subsets <math>I \subseteq \{ 1, \ldots, n \}</math> with exactly ''k'' elements.

De Gua's theorem and its generalisation (above) to ''n''-simplices with right-angle corners correspond to the special case where ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''n''&minus;1 and ''U'' is an (''n''−1)-simplex in <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> with vertices on the [[Cartesian coordinate system|co-ordinate axes]].  For example, suppose {{math|1=''n'' = 3}}, {{math|1=''k'' = 2}} and ''U'' is the [[triangle]] <math>\triangle ABC</math> in <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math> with vertices ''A'', ''B'' and ''C'' lying on the <math>x_1</math>-, <math>x_2</math>- and <math>x_3</math>-axes, respectively.  The subsets <math>I</math> of <math>\{ 1, 2, 3 \}</math> with exactly 2 elements are <math>\{ 2,3 \}</math>, <math>\{ 1,3 \}</math> and <math>\{ 1,2 \}</math>.  By definition, <math>U_{\{ 2,3 \}}</math> is the orthogonal projection of <math>U = \triangle ABC</math> onto the <math>x_2 x_3</math>-plane, so <math>U_{\{ 2,3 \}}</math> is the triangle <math>\triangle OBC</math> with vertices ''O'', ''B'' and ''C'', where ''O'' is the [[Origin (mathematics)#Cartesian coordinates|origin]] of <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math>.  Similarly, <math>U_{\{ 1,3 \}} = \triangle AOC</math> and <math>U_{\{ 1,2 \}} = \triangle ABO</math>, so the Conant–Beyer theorem says

<math display="block">\operatorname{vol}_2^2(\triangle ABC) = \operatorname{vol}_2^2(\triangle OBC) + \operatorname{vol}_2^2(\triangle AOC) + \operatorname{vol}_2^2(\triangle ABO),</math>
which is de Gua's theorem.

The generalisation of de Gua's theorem to ''n''-simplices with right-angle corners can also be obtained as a special case from the [[Cayley–Menger_determinant |Cayley–Menger determinant formula]].

De Gua's theorem can also be generalized to arbitrary tetrahedra and to pyramids, similarly to how the [[law of cosines]] generalises Pythagoras' theorem.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kheyfits |first1=Alexander |year=2004 |title=The Theorem of Cosines for Pyramids |journal=The College Mathematics Journal |publisher=Mathematical Association of America |volume=35 |issue=5 |pages=385–388 |doi=10.2307/4146849 |jstor=4146849}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tran |first=Quang Hung |date=2023-08-02 |title=A Generalization of de Gua's Theorem with a Vector Proof |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00283-023-10288-0 |journal=The Mathematical Intelligencer |volume=46 |issue=3 |pages=236–238 |language=en |doi=10.1007/s00283-023-10288-0 |issn=0343-6993|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==History==
Jean Paul de Gua de Malves (1713–1785) published the theorem in 1783, but around the same time a slightly more general version was published by another French mathematician, [[Charles de Tinseau d'Amondans]] (1746–1818), as well. However the theorem had also  been known much earlier to [[Johann Faulhaber]] (1580–1635) and [[René Descartes]] (1596–1650).<ref>{{MathWorld|title=de Gua's theorem|urlname=deGuasTheorem}}</ref><ref>Howard Whitley Eves: ''Great Moments in Mathematics (before 1650)''. Mathematical Association of America, 1983, {{ISBN|9780883853108}}, S. 37 ({{Google books|9_w5jDPTvCQC|excerpt|page=37}})</ref>
